quickAnswer: Gordion sits 95 km southwest of central Ankara near Polatlı, roughly 1 hour 15 minutes by private car. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023, the former Phrygian capital combines the 50-metre-high Great Tumulus (Tumulus MM), the oldest standing wooden tomb chamber known, the Gordion Museum, and the Iron Age Citadel Mound—easily visited in 2.5 to 3.5 hours.

body.text: Travelers planning a gordion midas ankara day trip often underestimate how accessible and well-organized the site is. Located beside the quiet village of Yassıhöyük, Gordion pairs naturally with a morning or afternoon at Ankara's Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, turning a capital transit stop into a complete Iron Age history study.
How far is Gordion from Ankara by private car?

Gordion is approximately 95 km southwest of central Ankara (Kızılay or Çankaya) and 125 km from Esenboğa Airport (ESB). By private car along the smooth E90/D200 highway toward Polatlı, the drive takes 70 to 85 minutes from downtown Ankara or about 1 hour 45 minutes directly from the airport.

Because public buses drop passengers in Polatlı—still 18 km short of Yassıhöyük village—hiring a private car or driver is far more efficient. You also need a vehicle on-site to move smoothly between the Gordion Museum, Tumulus MM, and the Citadel Mound roughly 1 km away.

body.text: What can you see inside the Great Tumulus and Gordion Museum?

Inside the Great Tumulus (Tumulus MM), a 70-metre concrete tunnel leads to a glass-fronted view of a circa 740 BCE juniper-and-pine log burial chamber—the oldest standing wooden structure of its kind. Across the road, the [Gordion Museum](https://muze.gov.tr/muze-detay?SectionId=GOR02&DistId=MRK) displays chronological Bronze Age, Phrygian, Greek, Hellenistic, and Roman artifacts, seals, and coins.

According to the [University of Pennsylvania's Gordion Tumulus MM guide](https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~nmiller0/Tour_MM_circuit.html), the Great Tumulus still stands over 50 metres tall and 300 metres wide—the largest of more than 100 ancient burial mounds dotting the Sakarya River plain. Tree-ring dating places the tomb around 740 BCE, meaning it was almost certainly built for King Midas's father (likely Gordias) rather than Midas himself.

Established in 1963 beside Yassıhöyük, the Gordion Museum showcases handmade Early Iron Age ceramics, textile-production tools, a panoramic reconstruction of the circa 700 BCE destruction layer, and imported Greek pottery. Note that the most famous inlaid wooden furniture and bronze banquet vessels recovered from Tumulus MM are exhibited in downtown Ankara at the [Museum of Anatolian Civilizations](https://muze.gov.tr/muze-detay?SectionId=AMM01&DistId=AMM), making a combined itinerary deeply rewarding.
Why did UNESCO inscribe Gordion as a World Heritage Site?

UNESCO inscribed [Gordion on the World Heritage List](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1669/) in September 2023 under Criterion (iii) as exceptional testimony to the Iron Age Kingdom of Phrygia. Covering 1,064 hectares with a 4,430-hectare buffer zone, the site preserves the Citadel Mound, fortified 10-metre-high Early Phrygian stone gate, Lower and Outer Towns, and surrounding royal tumuli.

UNESCO's evaluation highlighted both the integrity of Gordion's open rural setting and the survival of the best-preserved Iron Age (10th–8th century BCE) fortified citadel gate complex discovered in the Near East. Visitors walking the Citadel Mound can still see sloped stone masonry walls, megaron-plan royal halls, and pebble mosaic floors that predate Greek classical mosaics. Gordion is also famed in classical accounts as the city where Alexander the Great cut the Gordian Knot in 333 BCE.
How long does the visit take?

Plan 2.5 to 3.5 hours on-site at Gordion: 45 minutes inside the Gordion Museum, 30 to 45 minutes walking the tunnel into Tumulus MM and circling its exterior, and 60 to 90 minutes exploring the Citadel Mound and Phrygian Gate. Including round-trip transfers from Ankara, a comfortable half-day outing takes 5 to 6 hours.

items: Start at the Gordion Museum first to understand the Phrygian timeline before entering the tumulus tunnel.
Bring a light jacket for the Tumulus MM tunnel; interior air stays cool even in July and August.
Wear sturdy closed-toe shoes for gravel paths and uneven stone steps on the Citadel Mound.
Pair your morning Gordion visit with an afternoon at Ankara's Museum of Anatolian Civilizations to see the royal bronze and wood finds.

In winter, check windchill and daylight hours on the exposed Anatolian steppe; see our [Türkiye winter travel guide](https://itineraryofturkiye.com/blog/turkey-in-winter-premium-travel-guide) for cold-season routing tips.

faq.q: Was King Midas actually buried inside Tumulus MM?
faq.a: Dendrochronology dates the wooden chamber timbers to circa 740 BCE, suggesting the burial belonged to King Midas's father rather than the historical Midas who ruled later in the 8th century BCE.

faq.q: Are the Great Tumulus, Museum, and Citadel Mound covered by one ticket?
faq.a: Yes. A single admission ticket (or eligible MuseumPass) grants access to the Gordion Museum, Tumulus MM, and the Citadel Mound; confirm current pricing and seasonal hours on [Muze.gov.tr](https://muze.gov.tr/muze-detay?SectionId=GOR02&DistId=MRK).

faq.q: Is Gordion accessible for visitors with limited mobility?
faq.a: The Gordion Museum and the flat concrete approach tunnel into Tumulus MM are relatively accessible, though the Citadel Mound involves unpaved slopes and steps.

faq.q: Can I combine Gordion with Hattusha in a single day from Ankara?
faq.a: No. Gordion lies 95 km southwest of Ankara while Hattusha sits roughly 200 km east; combining both in one day means over 6 hours of driving and rushed sightseeing.

faq.q: Are there good lunch spots near Gordion?
faq.a: Yassıhöyük village offers simple tea gardens and basic gözleme spots. For full-service dining, stop in Polatlı (20 minutes away) or return to Ankara for a late lunch.

faq.q: What is the best season to visit Gordion?
faq.a: April through June and September through October deliver mild steppe temperatures and clear visibility across the burial mounds, avoiding summer midday heat and winter steppe winds.
